title: 10. Where the research goes from here
text:
Note



Key points for discussion, 2026-11-18. To be developed into a full section.


The goal of this work is practical. It aims to give local foundations and governments that want to strengthen their nonprofit sectors a defensible way to:

benchmark the sector against comparable places;
understand which conditions are associated with a stronger sector;
judge what their own investments can and cannot be expected to change.

The database and multiverse are the foundation. This page lists what is still open and what new data, methods and analyses would move the work toward that goal.

What the work already offers a community

A fair benchmark. A place’s density relative to its size-expected level (its SAMI) compares like with like, so a small town is not judged against a large city (Bettencourt et al., 2010). Counts scale linearly with population but spending does not, so per-capita spending is a misleading yardstick.
Realistic time horizons. Density is nearly frozen over decades. After population growth, the sector catches up slowly: half the gap closes in about 5 years for filers and 9 for grassroots. A five-year grant cycle should not expect to move the level.
Robust versus fragile levers.

Some associations are positive in most designs. Education is the most robust, followed by foundation assets and government money that flows through Medicaid and public payroll.
Others flip sign with the design. A community should not build strategy on the fragile ones (Part 8, Findings).

Two sectors, not one. Established filers follow the local economy. Grassroots organizations follow endowment and demography. Each responds to different conditions, and investments may reach one and not the other.



Open questions

What is causal? Nothing here is causal yet. The associations describe where strong sectors are, not what would make a sector stronger. This is the main gap for funders and governments, who need to know the effect of an action.
Why the regional gap? The Northeast has more than twice the South’s nonprofit employment per resident, with similar for-profit employment. The leading explanation is institutional: who owns hospitals, and how states contract for services (Salamon, 1987). It has not been tested.
How do grassroots organizations become established ones? Filer catch-up comes from existing organizations crossing the filing floor, not from new registrations. The pipeline from registration to a sustained, filing organization is the stage most open to local capacity-building, and it is the least understood.
Do shocks reset the sector? The metros that rose fastest include several hit by disasters (New Orleans, Gulfport, Santa Rosa, Chico, Redding). Whether disaster recovery builds lasting capacity is still a hypothesis.
Does giving respond to tax policy locally? Itemized contributions break at the 2018 tax change (the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), so individual giving’s role is unresolved until that break is modelled.
Size versus number. Is a community better served by more organizations or by larger ones? Counts and spending answer differently, and the right target depends on the community’s goal.



New data

Government funding received by nonprofits. The Form 990 government-grants line is in the e-file data from 2020. It was missing from the 2011–2019 extracts, so a consistent series has to be built from the e-file years forward. That would measure the delivery channel directly, rather than through Medicaid and public payroll.
Hospital ownership and state contracting. The American Hospital Association survey, CMS Provider of Services files and Medicaid managed-care contracts would test the institutional explanation of the regional gap.
Small organizations. Form 990-N (e-Postcard) filings and Form 1023-EZ approvals show which grassroots organizations are active and when new ones form. They would give a direct view of the registration-to-filer pipeline.
Local investments. Foundation grants by recipient location (990-PF Schedule and 990 Schedule I grants), plus community-foundation and local-government capacity-building programs. These are the “treatments” a causal design needs.
Nonprofit employment after 2022. The BLS research series ends in 2022, with no update announced before 2029. QCEW ownership codes or state unemployment-insurance records could extend it.



New methods

Designs for causal effects:

event studies around shocks (disasters, plant closures, hospital conversions that create health-conversion foundations);
synthetic control for single communities that launched a sector-building initiative;
difference-in-differences across staggered state policy changes.

Stock-flow models. Model entry, exit and growth across the filing floor separately, so that a community can see which flow drives its gap.
Small-area estimation. Most counties are small, and their densities are noisy. Multilevel models with partial pooling would give stable benchmarks for rural places, where funders often have the least information.
Multiverse for causal designs. The decision framework applies equally to causal estimates. Treatment timing, comparison group and outcome window are choices that should be crossed and reported (Steegen et al., 2016; Young & Holsteen, 2017).



Analyses that would serve funders and governments

A community benchmark tool. Built on this database, it would show:

each county’s and metro’s filer, grassroots and spending SAMIs, and their trajectories since 2000;
its position among peer places matched on size, region and growth history;
its subsector mix against need (for example, human-services density relative to poverty).

Gap diagnosis. Decompose a community’s gap into history (the pre-1970 endowment), recent growth (the catch-up lag) and current conditions. Only the last can be acted on.
Capacity indicators. Track the share of registered organizations that file, the rate of crossing the filing floor, and survival after formation. These are leading indicators that move faster than density itself.
Evaluation guidance. Translate the decision cards into a checklist for funders commissioning research:

which design choices change the answer;
which only look like robustness checks;
what time horizon an evaluation needs.




References


Bettencourt, L. M. A., Lobo, J., Strumsky, D., & West, G. B. (2010). Urban scaling and its deviations: Revealing the structure of wealth, innovation and crime across cities. PLoS ONE, 5(11), e13541. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0013541


Salamon, L. M. (1987). Of market failure, voluntary failure, and third-party government: Toward a theory of government-nonprofit relations in the modern welfare state. Journal of Voluntary Action Research, 16(1–2), 29–49.


Steegen, S., Tuerlinckx, F., Gelman, A., & Vanpaemel, W. (2016). Increasing transparency through a multiverse analysis. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(5), 702–712.


Young, C., & Holsteen, K. (2017). Model uncertainty and robustness: A computational framework for multimodel analysis. Sociological Methods & Research, 46(1), 3–40.

title: Findings
text: Five findings. All results are from run v11: 432,432 specifications of the 13-covariate model of 02-variables.qmd, over 387 metros and 925 CBSAs, 2010–2022. The registered-stock specifications were also refit with grassroots (registered public charities that do not file above the floor) as the outcome. Every summary here reports filers, grassroots and spending separately. The two count populations disagree on several covariates (D1), so a “counts” summary that pools them averages opposite answers.

title: Stylized Facts about Nonprofit Density Data
text:
Seven regularities hold in metro-level 501(c)(3) density data before any covariate enters a model. Each is descriptive, and together they motivate the design decisions in the decision cards (D1–D12, in 04-design-decisions.qmd). Data cover 387 US metros, 2000–2024, unless noted.

Counts scale proportionally; spending scales faster and depends on the unit.

Full-sector counts: β ≈ 1.00 at every aggregation (county, metro, metro + micro, CSA) and under OLS and Poisson (range 0.01–0.02).
Counts look sublinear (β ≈ 0.88) only after conditioning on covariates.
Spending: county 1.46 → metro 1.27 → CSA 1.23 (OLS). Big-budget organizations sit in core counties.
Subsectors differ: human services and environment are sublinear (0.90–0.96); education, religion-related and international are superlinear (1.07–1.21).

Density is nearly frozen.

Filer SAMIs correlate .94 twenty years apart; 97.5% of their variance is between metros.
No convergence: the cross-metro SD is .40 in both 2000 and 2024; λ = −.064 over 24 years (half-life about 240 years).
Filer density is more persistent than metro GDP.

Density lags population, but differently within and across metros.

Within a metro, half of size-expected organizations are missing right after growth. The gap closes with a half-life of about 5 years (filers) and 9 years (grassroots) in local projections, and about 10 and 7.5 years in kernel (distributed-lag) models in levels.
Across metros, the Sunbelt deficit (about −25% for the fastest-growing fifth) predates 2000, tracks 1970–2000 growth, and closes only once growth slows (half-life about 35 years). Stock-flow accounting shows it is a lag, not a trait: fast growers add at least as many entrants per resident as other metros, and growth alone produces the gap.
Decline is asymmetric: organizations stay at first, then grassroots shed the excess (half-life about 4 years). Relative income losses lower filer density immediately; gains do nothing.

Filers and grassroots are two populations.

Grassroots (registered non-filers) are 72–80% of the registered stock and also scale at about 1.0.
Filers follow the local economy (income, wages, market share) and do not converge across metros.
Grassroots follow endowment and demography and converge (half-life about 27 years).
Filer catch-up comes from existing organizations crossing the filing floor, not from new registrations.

Nonprofit market share sets the level, not the pace.

Share of private employment (BLS) explains about a third of the density percentile and absorbs the growth-history effect.
It is at most a soft ceiling on catch-up (grassroots only). Regions differ in its level, not its change.
It partly measures the outcome: it includes hospitals and universities and rises with density. The regional gap in share is mostly ownership: the Northeast has 61 nonprofit jobs per 1,000 residents, the South 25, with similar for-profit employment.
Older sectors hold larger shares. Northeast and Midwest filers are about 3.5 years older than those in the South and West, and Northeast filers last longest. Within the South and West, each extra year of average filer age goes with about 6% more share.

Size is the main source of collinearity.

In log form, size-scaled covariates correlate .80–.94 with log population (2022 metros); the SAMI transformation removes it (largest VIF 2.2 in the default model).
Entering every candidate measure at once makes blocks cancel; one composite per block recovers them.

Data hazards are frequent and patterned.

Source splices (CORE → SOI in 2011, SOI → e-file in 2020) move spending SAMIs, not counts. TY2020 counts are about 9% low.
Group exemptions inflate a few metros (Memphis, Mankato).
Panel covariates are often interpolated (turnout observed in 23% of metro-years; ACS rolling averages).
Itemized contributions break at the 2018 tax change; association counts and the Rupasingha index partly count nonprofits. A total with zeros (foundation assets in Eagle Pass, TX) becomes a leverage point under log(1 + x).



Fact 1: Counts scale proportionally, spending does not
Organization counts grow in proportion to population; spending grows faster, and how much faster depends on the geographic unit. This one fact decides whether per-capita measures are safe.
Evidence 1: two exponents, two verdicts on per capita (387 metros, 2022).

Filers scale at β = 0.99. Filers per capita change by −3% per tenfold increase in population, and size explains 0.1% of their variance. The SAMI and log filers per capita correlate .999.
Spending (excluding hospitals and universities) scales at β = 1.29. Spending per resident rises 95% per tenfold increase in population, and size explains 16% of its variance. The SAMI and log spending per capita correlate only .92.

What it means for practice.

Report β for the outcome, unit and estimator used, and say whether it is bivariate or conditional.
Full-sector counts per capita are acceptable at the metro level; spending per capita is not. For spending, use log-log or SAMI forms (D4).
Compare exponents only across studies that use the same unit: county spending exponents run about 0.2 above metro ones.
Use Poisson whenever zeros are common (subsectors, small units).

Evidence 2: almost all the variation is between metros.

97.5% of the variance in the filer SAMI is between metros. Within a metro its SD is about 0.06 log points, against 0.39 overall.
A growth-curve model gives an SD of 0.38 for metro levels and 0.06 per decade for metro trends, with no relation between them (r = −.04).
Covariates are just as fixed: within-metro shares of variance over 2010–2022 are 0.2% for % nonwhite, 0.8% for % BA, 3.3% for turnout and 6.7% for foundation assets, and much of that is interpolation.

Evidence 3: no convergence for filers.

The SD of the filer SAMI was .40 in 2000, .38 in 2015 and .40 in 2024.
Regressing the 2000–2024 change on the 2000 level gives λ = −.064, a half-life of about 240 years. Instrumenting the 2000 level with the independent registered-stock measure gives −.060, so this is not measurement error.
Grassroots narrowed slightly (SD .31 to .26; half-life about 27 years). Spending widened (.66 to .75).

Climbers include New Orleans (+33 percentile points), Chico (+31) and Cleveland TN (+28); decliners include Decatur IL and Hagerstown (−33 each) and Tyler (−29). These changes are real but noisy: the 24-year change correlates .62 with the 2011–2024 change and .41 with the change in the registered-stock SAMI.

What it means for practice.

Within-metro designs work with about 2.5% of the outcome’s variance and mostly interpolated covariate change. Treat them as weakly identified (D3).
Pooling years adds little beyond a single cross-section. Do not count metro-years as independent: cluster by metro and count degrees of freedom in metros.
A single recent year represents a metro’s long-run filer density well. For spending, average several years and avoid splice years.
Persistence makes history a confounder in levels models: today’s covariates partly stand in for conditions decades ago (Fact 3, D8).

Figure 7: Change in mean SAMI since 2000 by growth quintile, on one shared scale. Each quintile is re-based to 0 in 2000. Filers stay within ±2% over 24 years in every quintile: fast growers kept pace with their own growth but never closed the inherited gap. Grassroots fan out by about ±9%.




The fastest-growing fifth sits about 25% below size-expected density in every year, although new growth after 2000 was matched almost one-for-one.
The same holds in dollars. The median fastest-fifth metro spent $812 per resident in 2000 and $1,803 in 2024 (real 2022 dollars, excluding hospitals and universities), 30–45% below the other quintiles in both years. Its spending grew as fast as everyone else’s (+133% vs. +126% for all metros): no catch-up and no further falling behind.
The 2000 gap tracks 1970–2000 growth (−.36 per log point, with region and census traits controlled; R² .63). Recent decades weigh more than older ones, as a lag would.
The within-metro rates explain only about a quarter of the fastest fifth’s filer gap. Fast growers whose growth slowed after 2000 closed about a third of their gap in 24 years (half-life about 35 years); those still growing fast closed none.
The growth-history gap does not survive nonprofit market share: fast growers also have small nonprofit workforces, and the two cannot be separated in a cross-section.

Evidence 2b: lag or trait? The flows say lag. A stock gains entrants and loses exits: dN/dt = fP − dN, where f is entrants per resident and d the exit rate. A metro whose flows held steady would settle at density f / (d + g), where g is population growth. That steady state splits exactly into three parts: entry per resident, the exit rate, and growth. Only the growth part is a lag: the stock trails a population that keeps arriving. A trait of in-migration would show as fewer entrants per resident or faster exit. The test uses 2012–13 to 2018–19, within one data source (SOI), so no splice enters.

Still-growing fast growers are short because of growth alone. They add more entrants per resident than other metros (+.13), not fewer, and lose them a little faster (−.06). Growth (−.28) accounts for the whole gap. They sit at their own steady state (+.04, n.s.): the gap stays as long as growth does.
Slowed growers have normal flows but an inherited deficit. Entry and exit match other metros, so their flows would sustain average density. They sit about 10% below that level (−.10, SE .06; −.11 with region fixed effects). That is the signature of a lag: the gap should close, at a half-life of about 16 years if 2012–19 flows hold. That is faster than the roughly 35 years observed over 2000–2024.
1970–2000 growth leaves no trace in the flows. Entry per resident rises with current growth and dips after growth in 2000–12, as newcomers take time to form or join organizations. Net of both and of region, 1970–2000 growth predicts nothing: +.01 (SE .10) for filers and +.01 (SE .06) for registrations. Exit rates track none of the growth measures.
Registrations tell the same story with one twist. Still-growing fast growers sit 13% above the steady state their flows imply, so their registered density should keep falling while growth continues, as the grassroots trajectories show.
Entry carries most cross-metro differences. The steady state correlates .79 with observed filer density; entry alone correlates .78. The lowest-entry metros are border metros (Laredo, McAllen, Eagle Pass, Yuma), a trait not tied to growth history.
Limits. Entry counts new organizations, moves in and, for filers, organizations crossing the revenue floor. The test rules out lower entry or faster exit as the source of the fast growers’ gap. It cannot rule out a trait that works only through growth itself, and it says nothing about why fast growers have small nonprofit market shares.

Evidence 3: decline and income losses work differently.

Population decline: organizations stay at first, so density rises. Filers realize only a third of the size-expected decline within five years, against three quarters of expected growth; grassroots then shed the excess, which halves in about 4 years and is gone by year 8, roughly twice as fast as they fill a growth shortfall.
Relative income loss: a 10% loss lowers filer density by about 1.5–2% at once, recovering with a half-life of about 10 years. Relative income gains do nothing, and registrations do not respond either way.

Evidence 4: catch-up runs through existing organizations. After growth, new registrations do not rise within a metro. Instead, the share of registered organizations that file climbs for 6–10 years: existing organizations grow past the filing thresholds and appear in the 990 data.

A fixed lag is the wrong shape. For filers every single lag of population fits worse than current population, and adding one growth window captures less than half of what the kernel gains.
Grassroots never fully catch up within a metro (β = .72). Imposing the cross-sectional slope (.99), as a SAMI outcome does, turns that shortfall into slow adjustment and inflates their half-life to 40 years. Put log P and G on the right instead.
The kernel (about 10 years) and the local projections (about 5) agree for five years after growth, then part: the kernel keeps a small deficit (filers −2.5% at year 10). The difference is metro-specific trends, which 25 years of data cannot separate from a slow tail, so the two estimates bound the within-metro half-life.
Organizations barely leave after population loss: separate gain and loss kernels fit filers best, with about 90% of an implied decline unrealized at first.
In the multiverse the kernel enters as a covariate (D8, Evidence 5).

What it means for practice.

Annual within-metro models estimate a short-run adjustment that is half closed in about five years. Do not read them as long-run effects.
For change questions, use differences of 10 years or more, or include a geometric kernel of past population change (half-life 5–10 years) rather than a fixed lag, and model growth and decline separately.

For spending it drops to .87 in 2011 (.90 excluding hospitals and universities) and .94 in 2020, against .99 in other years and .98–.99 for metro GDP and income. Grassroots dip to .95 in 2017–18, where BMF snapshots omit newly ruled organizations.
Evidence 3: most covariate-years are filled in. Share of metro-years observed rather than interpolated or carried forward, 2000–2024:

% BA, % foreign born and Gini: 64% (ACS five-year estimates in recent years, the census before that).
Contributions: 56%, and only 2010–2023.
Turnout and Democratic margin: 28% (presidential election years only).
The 2020 and 2024 returns come from a news-feed compilation and match official sources. Harris and Trump county votes equal MIT’s official 2024 precinct returns; metro votes, margins and SAMI-form turnout correlate 1.000 (296 metros). The compilation omits some minor-candidate votes, so a few state totals run 0.5–2% low in 2024 (New York 2.2%), and Kansas runs 1.8% low in 2020. The check found one real error, in the 2016 official file: Bedford County, VA was double-counted, which made Lynchburg the highest-turnout metro in 2016 (.83 instead of .62). It is now fixed; correlations with filer density move by .002 at most.
Social capital measures: 16% (waves through 2014). Religion: 12% (decennial).

Within-metro and lag models fit mostly interpolated change in these covariates (D3).
Evidence 4: registration practices distort the registered stock. Group-exemption subordinates registered at a headquarters address inflate Memphis and Mankato. Military towns (Augusta, Hinesville, Fayetteville, Warner Robins, Sumter) register far more charities than their filer counts imply. LDS congregations that do not register separately keep Utah low. These distort counts, not covariate results: dropping Memphis and Mankato moves no benchmark (D2, Evidence 5).
Evidence 5: some covariates partly count the outcome. The Rupasingha social-capital index includes NCCS nonprofit density and turnout; its revised version and CBP association counts still include membership organizations, which are mostly nonprofits. Market share counts the employees of the organizations being counted (Fact 5).
Evidence 6: the 2018 tax law moves contribution coefficients, though not contribution rankings. The 13-covariate default model was refit as a metro cross-section in every year 2010–2022, with each contribution measure in place of foundation assets:

Metro rankings survive the break. Year-to-year rank correlations across metros are .966 for contributions per return and per capita across 2017–18, against about .98 in other years (.936 vs. .97 for contributions as a share of AGI).
Coefficients shift, more than in the six-covariate model.

For filer counts, total contributions go from a partial r of .01 before 2018 to .16 after (OLS), and from −.01 to .14 with division FE. These jumps are 5–7 times their year-to-year SD before 2018; the six-covariate model gave .005 → .058.
Contributions per return and as a share of AGI go from slightly negative (−.03 to −.08) to positive (.04 to .11), so their sign depends on the year.
For spending the jumps are .08–.10.
The other covariates in the same models move by at most .05 (2.8 SD; turnout and % nonwhite in spending models). Foundation assets in the default model move by .03 or less (1 SD).

Within metros the break carries part of the estimate. A contribution × post-2018 term is significant for share of AGI (t = 3.5, counts) and for total contributions (t = 3.4 for spending, −2.2 for counts).
Every multiverse cross-section (2019, 2022) is after the law, so its contribution results describe the post-2018 itemizing slice. The pooled (2015–22) and within (2010–22) contribution specifications span the break.

Evidence 6b: what the law does to the multiverse. Every contribution specification in run v11 (34,914, excluding 2019 cross-sections; 13-covariate model) was refit on a pre-2018 window: a 2017 cross-section instead of 2022, pooled 2015–17 instead of 2015–22, within 2010–17 instead of 2010–22. Each default twin (foundation assets) was refit the same way, so the window’s own effect can be subtracted.

Contribution terms, cross-section, counts: +.06 to +.08 after the law and about 0 before it (−.003 to .014). Net of the window effect, the law adds .05; the six-covariate model gave .03–.04. Signs flip in 11–22% of specifications.

The share significant rises most for share of AGI (17% → 34%) and less for the other two measures (30–39% → 37–46%).

Pooled counts: the law adds .03–.035. Spending: the law lowers the contribution terms by .02 or less.
Within metros: contribution estimates are unstable whatever the window. Their partial r correlates only −.40 to .40 between the two windows for counts and .47 to .65 for spending, so within-metro contribution results should not be reported as findings.
The other 12 covariates: swapping contributions in for foundation assets moves them by at most .023 more under the full window than under the pre-2018 one (the Gini in count cross-sections); the median shift is .01 or less.
For the paper: one note. Individual giving is weak in every window. Post-2018 cross-sections make it look stronger, because itemizers became a smaller, richer group. Within-metro giving effects are not identified.

Evidence 7: zeros in a size-scaled covariate create leverage points. Eagle Pass, TX has no foundation assets in any year; under log(1 + x) it sat about 11 SD below the metro mean and drove spurious interactions (D6, Evidence 6).






Figure 20: Data hazards. (A) 387-metro totals indexed to 2010 for filers, filers without a floor, registered stock, spending and contributions, with source changes marked. (B) Year-to-year SAMI correlations by year. (C) Share of metro-years observed for each covariate. (D) Registered-stock SAMI against filer SAMI in 2022, with outliers labeled.



What it means for practice.

Use year fixed effects in every panel and never read a change across 2011 or 2020 as real without a check against counts.
For spending cross-sections, avoid 2011 and 2020, or average several years.
Treat tax year 2020 counts as low; drop or flag them in change and lag models.
Do not let contributions models span 2018, and do not compare contribution coefficients across it. Read the multiverse’s pooled and within contribution specifications as flagged.
Report the observed share of each covariate, and prefer models that use observed years (election years, census years) over interpolated panels.
Exclude covariates built from nonprofit counts (Rupasingha index, association counts) from models of nonprofit density.
Check registered and grassroots outcomes for group-exemption and military-town outliers before interpreting them.

title: Design Decisions
text:
Twelve cards, ordered from the choices that define the question to the choices that only refine it. Every card is read on the 13-covariate model of 02-variables.qmd: poverty and % 65+ (need); the metro Gini, % nonwhite, religious fractionalization and age SD (heterogeneity); foundation assets, % BA and turnout (supply); the 10-year growth kernel, state and local government earnings, Medicaid and the pre-1970 endowment (market niche). The evidence comes from two sources. Single models refit each option with the 13 covariates on 385 metros (Memphis and Mankato have no endowment value). Run v11 of the multiverse supplies the distributions: the same forks as before, with the 13-covariate model as the default, one-at-a-time measurement swaps and drop-one-block contrasts, 432,432 specifications in all.
What the 13-covariate model changes across the cards.

Poverty is clearly negative for filers (partial r −.29, against −.10 in the old six-covariate model). It no longer changes sign between filers and grassroots (D1), and it no longer reverses with metro size (D2).
Foundation assets roughly halve (.41 → .21 for filers, .26 → .11 for spending). No single term absorbs them; the endowment, Medicaid and the heterogeneity terms share it.
Turnout is a grassroots covariate. It is about zero for filers (.01) and spending (.04) and .24 for grassroots.
% BA strengthens (.24 → .37 for filers), and % nonwhite weakens a little (−.26 → −.20) and turns positive for grassroots (+.13).
The most estimator-sensitive terms are now the new state-patterned ones: Medicaid (.24 under OLS, .06 within states) and religious fractionalization (.12 → .00).

Old values are from the six-covariate cards; refitting the old model on the current data and the same 385 metros moves them by .02 or less, so the changes are the model’s, not the data’s.

D1. Outcome population: filers, grassroots, registered stock, or spending
Decision. Which population of organizations “density” counts: established filers, grassroots organizations, the whole registered stock, or the money they spend.
Type. Estimand choice. Each population answers a different question, and the choice changes signs.
Options.

Filers: 501(c)(3) public charities filing a 990 or 990-EZ with revenue or expenses of at least $50k (2010 dollars). The established, economically active sector.
Grassroots: registered public charities that do not file at that level: postcard (990-N) filers, small filers, registered churches and dormant registrations. 72–80% of the registered stock.
Registered stock: the IRS Business Master File (BMF), both groups together.
Spending: expenses or revenue, gross or net of pass-through grants, with or without hospitals and universities.
Congregations that never register are outside every count.

Mechanism. The populations grow for different reasons. Filers follow the local economy, because organizations cross the filing floor as their revenue grows. Grassroots follow demography and institutional legacy. Spending is dominated by a few large organizations and scales faster than population.
Evidence 1: the populations rank metros differently (387 metros, 2022).

Filer and grassroots SAMIs correlate .67. The registered stock correlates .97 with grassroots but .83 with filers, so it mostly measures grassroots.
Spending correlates .71 with filers and .41 with grassroots.
All three counts scale at about 1.0 (filers 0.99, grassroots 1.01, registered 1.00); spending scales at 1.29. The SAMI spreads differ: SD .39 for filers, .26 for grassroots, .73 for spending.

Evidence 3: in the multiverse, outcome population is the largest decision for filers. Grassroots were added to the multiverse by refitting every registered-stock specification of run v11 with registered non-filers as the outcome.

η²: filers vs. grassroots explains .69 of the spread for % nonwhite, .58 for turnout, .57 for religious fractionalization, .46 for % BA, .42 for poverty and .29 for age SD. Counts vs. spending explains .57 for poverty and .36 for % 65+.
Default-model medians, filers vs. grassroots: % nonwhite −.07 vs. +.11, turnout .08 vs. .21, religious fractionalization .09 vs. .28, % BA .31 vs. .16, poverty −.17 vs. −.07.
Impact: changing only the population changes 41% of covariate verdicts (|Δr| = .098), more than any other decision for filers. Between counts and spending it changes 37% (Section 13).

Evidence 4: the populations move differently over time (Facts 2 to 4).

Filers are more persistent (r = .94 at 20 years, vs. .78 for grassroots).
Filer gains follow income growth (partial r .35); grassroots gains do not (−.07).
Only filers respond to income losses: organizations drop below the filing floor into the grassroots count.
Grassroots deficits converge across metros (half-life about 27 years); filer deficits do not.
Nonprofit market share explains 35% of filer density but 14% of grassroots density.

Recommendation.

Match the population to the theory. Service capacity and economic-sector questions call for filers; civic participation and associational life call for grassroots, noting that unregistered congregations are missing; questions about the scale of resources call for spending.
Report filers and grassroots separately. The pooled registered stock is mostly grassroots and hides the cases where the two disagree (% nonwhite, Medicaid, religious fractionalization).
When counts and spending disagree, the finding concerns the number versus the size of organizations; it is not a robustness failure.
Check registered and grassroots counts for group-exemption artifacts (Memphis, Mankato).

What to report. The population definition (forms, floor, exclusions) and the key results for both filers and grassroots.

D2. Unit of analysis: county, metro, metro + micro, CSA
Decision. Which geographic unit carries the analysis: counties, metropolitan CBSAs, metro plus micropolitan CBSAs, micropolitan areas alone, CSAs, or counties compared within their metro.
Type. Estimand choice. Each unit asks a different question: how dense a market is, or where organizations locate inside one.
Options (2022):

Counties: 3,144, of which 3,090 have a filer.
Metro CBSAs: 387. Metro plus micro CBSAs: 925. Micropolitan only: 538.
CSA or metro (CSA where the metro belongs to one, else the metro): 271.
Counties within metros: 1,183 counties with metro fixed effects.

Mechanism. Counties split labor and service markets: an organization serving a whole metro is counted in its core county, and the 990 credits all its spending to its headquarters. Small units create zeros. Counties compared within a metro measure how organizations are arranged inside a market, not how many a market supports.
Evidence 1: the count exponent is stable; the spending exponent is not. Bivariate β for filers is 0.97–0.99 at every unit (1.10 for counties within metros). For spending it is 1.25–1.42 across units and 1.60 for counties within metros (Fact 1).

The multiverse agrees. The 1,212 default-model specifications per outcome (2022 and 2019 cross-sections and pooled; every DV form, predictor form, unit, estimator except state random effects, and winsorizing) were refit with the quadratic size interaction. For filers, poverty’s effect is concave in 94% of specifications and the size terms are jointly significant in 86%, but the effect is negative at every size: median t −4.7 at 100k (significantly negative in 93% of specifications), −2.7 at 250k, −0.8 at 1M and −0.7 at 4M. It is significantly positive at 1M in 2% of specifications, against 16% with six covariates. For grassroots poverty is negative in small metros (t −2.1 at 100k) and near zero above 250k; for spending it is near zero at every size.

The reversal was an omitted-variable pattern. In the six-covariate model poverty for filers was −.11 to −.14 in smaller metros and +.08 to +.13 in larger ones. With the 13 covariates it is negative and significant at every size; the curvature remains (concave, joint p .018) but bends a negative effect toward zero instead of across it. No single term does this: poverty correlates .34 with Medicaid and .36 with the Gini in SAMI form, and dropping either leaves large-metro poverty at −.16 to −.22.
Two size differences remain. Foundation assets for spending still peak at mid-size (concave, joint p .015). Turnout for filers is negative in smaller metros and positive in larger ones (−.08 vs .16, z = 2.4).

Recommendation.

For questions about density, use metro CBSAs or CSAs. They match labor and service markets, have no zeros and give similar answers.
Use counties only for questions about location within a market, with metro fixed effects, and say so: a positive poverty coefficient there means organizations sit where need concentrates inside a metro.
Do not pool micropolitan areas with metros without testing whether they behave alike.
Treat a population threshold like the unit: a choice of which places the claim covers. If a claim is meant for large cities, report it for metros of 250k or more as well.
Do not report the poverty-by-size reversal as a finding: it disappears once need, heterogeneity and indirect government are measured. Report the size split as a check.
Do not add case exclusions as a fork. One robustness line (dropping DC, Alaska and Hawaii, group-exemption metros and the size extremes) covers them.
Compare spending exponents only across studies that use the same unit.

D3. Identification: cross-section, between, within, long difference
Decision. Which variation identifies a covariate’s association: differences between metros (a cross-section, or pooled years with year FE), changes within metros (metro and year FE), or long-run change (long differences, growth curves), and whether to estimate between and within effects together (correlated random effects, hybrid models).
Type. Estimand choice. Between and within estimators answer different questions. They are not more and less robust versions of one answer.
Options.

Cross-section: one year, or an average of several.
Pooled panel with year FE: all years; mixes between and within variation, but between variation dominates.
Within: metro and year FE; only deviations from each metro’s own mean. The endowment drops out.
Long differences: change over 10–20 years regressed on covariate change, with the starting level.
Growth curves and hybrid models: metro means and deviations entered together, giving between and within effects in one model.
State or division FE (D9) sit in between: they remove regional levels but keep differences among metros within a state.

Mechanism. Density and its covariates are nearly fixed (Fact 2). A within estimator discards the 95–99% of variance that lies between metros and fits what is left: interpolated ACS change, source splices, and short-run adjustment that lags population change by years (Fact 3). A pooled estimator keeps the between variance and so reproduces the cross-section; counting metro-years as independent overstates the sample 8 to 13 times.

D4. DV form: per capita, log-log, SAMI, Poisson
Decision. How size enters the outcome: counts or dollars per capita (linear), log per capita, log Y with log P on the right (log-log), or the SAMI (the residual of log Y on log P).
Type. Avoidable error. A per capita form is a constraint on the size coefficient. When the constraint is wrong, the error flows into every covariate correlated with size.
Options.

Per capita, linear: organizations per 10,000 residents, dollars per resident. The most common form in the literature.
Log per capita: log(Y/P).
Log-log: log Y on log P plus covariates.
SAMI: the residual of log Y on log P, with covariates also in SAMI form. Identical to log-log by FWL (Fact 6).
Poisson with log P or a population offset: see D5.

Mechanism. log(Y/P) = log Y − log P, so a per capita model is a log-log model with the coefficient on log P fixed at 1. The constraint fails in two ways.

The outcome may not scale at 1. Spending scales at 1.29, so per capita spending still carries 0.29 × log P.
Even when Y scales at 1, the coefficient on log P is no longer 1 once size-bearing covariates enter the model (per capita foundation assets, government earnings, Medicaid). The constraint then pushes weight onto them.

In both cases the omitted size term biases each covariate in proportion to its correlation with size: % BA r = .40 with log P, foundation assets .42, % nonwhite .38, poverty −.23; among the new terms, the Gini .42, age SD −.33, the growth kernel .22 and the per capita endowment −.25.
Evidence 1: per capita ranks metros like the SAMI for counts, but by size for spending.

Filer counts scale at β = 0.99. Log per capita filers is flat in population (R² = .00), and per capita and SAMI ranks correlate .999.
Spending scales at 1.29. Per capita spending rises with population (R² = .16), and the ranks correlate .90.
The ten largest metros average the 77th percentile of per capita spending but the 39th percentile by SAMI. New York is 94th per capita vs. 51st by SAMI, Dallas 66th vs. 20th, Houston 54th vs. 12th.

D5. Estimator with zeros: OLS on logs vs. Poisson
Decision. How to estimate when some units have no organizations or no dollars: OLS on log Y with zeros dropped, OLS on log(Y + 1), or Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PML) with log P or a population offset.
Type. Avoidable error for subsectors, small units and changes in counts. For full-sector metro models, a weighting choice.
Options.

OLS on log Y, zeros dropped.
OLS on log(Y + 1) or another added constant.
Poisson PML with log P on the right (β estimated) or as an offset (β = 1), with robust SEs. It estimates the elasticity of the mean consistently without assuming the data are Poisson.
Negative binomial, hurdle or zero-inflated models, when the zero process is itself of interest.

Mechanism.

Dropping zeros keeps only the small places that happen to have an organization, which are the small places with unusually many. That flattens the slope.
log(Y + 1) pulls small counts toward zero and flattens it further.
Poisson keeps the zeros and models the mean on the original scale. It also weights units by their expected count, so large places dominate. That weighting matters even when there are no zeros.

D6. Predictor form for size-scaled covariates

Per capita: the total divided by population.
Logged total, with zeros raised to a per-capita floor before logging (see Evidence 6).

Recommendation.

Enter totals in SAMI form, or as logged totals with log P on the right, which is the same model.
Never enter raw dollars or raw counts.
Never log(1 + x) a total that has zeros. Floor it per capita at a low percentile of positive values first, and check the minimum z of every logged covariate.
Per capita is acceptable for totals that scale at about 1 (government earnings); check the size correlation first, since foundation assets and the endowment still carry size per capita.
Treat the outcome and the totals alike (D4). A SAMI outcome with logged totals and no log P re-creates the problem.
Keep the model additive. Report interactions as robustness checks, not forks.

What to report. The form of every size-scaled covariate, whether log P is on the right, and each total’s correlation with log P in the form used.

D8. Historical controls: endowment, growth history and market share
Decision. Whether to control for the sector’s own history (the pre-1970 endowment of charities), for the metro’s past population growth (the growth kernel), or for its current size in the labor market (the nonprofit share of private employment).
Type. Estimand choice, with a risk of bad controls. The endowment is the same organizations decades earlier, and market share counts the employees of today’s organizations. The growth kernel is built from population and carries no such risk.
Options.

Pre-1970 endowment: 501(c)(3) public charities in the 2000 BMF stock with a ruling date before 1970, in SAMI form; group-exemption artifacts (Memphis, Mankato) set to missing. In the 13-covariate default; the multiverse drops it as a contrast.
Growth kernel: a geometric memory of past log population change, G[t] = a·G[t−1] + Δlog P[t] with a = 0.5^(1/half-life), at a 10-year half-life (5-year as the swap), built from 1970–2024 population. In the default; it varies over time, so it also runs within metros.
Market share: the BLS 501(c)(3) share of private employment, averaged over 2013–2022. Not in the default.

Mechanism. Density is persistent (Fact 2), so any covariate that was high decades ago, and is still high, gets credit for density that arose then. The endowment soaks that up, and so it changes the question from “where is density high?” to “where is density higher than its history predicts?” Growth history does the same for the Sunbelt lag (Fact 3). Market share goes further: it overlaps the outcome in the present, so it absorbs any covariate that works through the size of the sector.

D9. Geography fixed effects and standard errors

D10. Money measure and exclusions
Decision. Which money to count: expenses or revenue; gross, or net of grants passed through to other organizations; and with or without hospitals and universities.
Type. Analyst discretion, of very different weight. The hospital and university exclusion changes results. The money measure mostly changes levels.
Options.

Expenses or revenue. Revenue is lumpier: 43% of organization-years change by more than 20%, against 36% for expenses.
Gross or net of pass-through: net subtracts grants paid to domestic organizations and governments (Form 990 Part IX line 1). Available from 2012.
All 501(c)(3) filers, or excluding hospitals and universities (NTEE E20–E24, B40–B43, B50, and the e-file industry codes; e-file NTEE codes backfilled from the BMF since 2026-11-17).

Mechanism.

Hospitals and universities are 47% of 501(c)(3) spending nationally, but the share ranges from almost nothing to 75% across metros (10th to 90th percentile). Whether a metro’s hospital and university count at all depends on ownership: public universities and government hospitals file no 990, and system hospitals may file at a headquarters elsewhere. An all-sector spending SAMI is largely a measure of that.
Pass-through money is concentrated in a few intermediaries (the top 1% of grantmaking charities pay 85–89% of grants to organizations), which sit disproportionately in large and educated metros.
Revenue and expenses differ year to year but describe the same organizations over a cross-section.

Spending SAMIs with and without hospitals and universities correlate .80, and the hospital and university share correlates .65 with the all-sector SAMI but .09 with the SAMI that excludes them. When the theory is about one kind of organization (government failure in human services, cultural demand for the arts), model that subsector directly, with Poisson.

title: 2. Dataset construction
text:
What the database measures
The database measures nonprofit density: the number and size of charitable nonprofits in a place, relative to what its population would predict. Density differs widely across US communities, and the reasons are much debated: unmet demand for public goods, the supply of resources and civic capacity, and the role of government (Lecy & Van Slyke, 2013). To test those explanations side by side, the database puts every 501(c)(3) public charity in the United States into a county and year, and joins it to about 300 covariates describing each place’s economy, demography, government, politics and civic life.
Two features drive the design:

Many sources, one geography. Nonprofit counts come from IRS registration files and three generations of financial-return data. Covariates come from about 20 federal and academic sources. Everything is placed on one fixed county geography and then aggregated to metropolitan areas.
Population sets the expected level. Larger places have more nonprofits almost exactly in proportion to population, but not more spending (Bettencourt et al., 2007). The analysis therefore compares places with their size-expected level (scale-adjusted metropolitan indicators, SAMIs) (Bettencourt et al., 2010). The database stores the counts and totals the SAMIs are computed from.



Units and coverage









Counties
Core-based statistical areas (CBSAs)

Every source is first placed on county-equivalents. The CBSA table sums counts and dollar totals over a CBSA’s counties, then recomputes rates and shares with the same formulas. Some measures exist only for metros (BLS nonprofit employment, market competition, the metro Gini, the pre-1970 endowment, population-lag kernels), which is why the CBSA table has 68 more columns. Choosing metros only or all CBSAs is a filter on cbsa_year, not a separate table.


The nonprofit outcomes
Four outcome populations come from the same organizations:

Filers: 501(c)(3) public charities that file a Form 990 or 990-EZ above an inflation-adjusted activity floor. Annual counts come from three generations of return data, spliced together:

NCCS CORE files for 2000–2010 (Urban Institute, National Center for Charitable Statistics, 2024);
IRS Statistics of Income exempt-organization extracts for 2011–2019 (Internal Revenue Service, Statistics of Income, 2025a);
NCCS e-file data for 2020–2024 (Urban Institute, National Center for Charitable Statistics, 2026a).

Registered stock: every public charity on the IRS Business Master File in a given year, from the NCCS legacy snapshots for 2000–2022 and the monthly BMF for 2023–2024 (Urban Institute, National Center for Charitable Statistics, 2023, 2025).
Grassroots: registered charities that do not file above the floor (registered stock minus filers). They are 72–80% of the registered stock.
Spending: total expenses of filers, in 2022 dollars, deflated with the PCE price index (U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, 2026a).

Each organization is located with the geocoded unified BMF (Urban Institute, National Center for Charitable Statistics, 2026b). Its subsector comes from its NTEE code. Invalid codes (UND, INV, Z99) are replaced once, from each organization’s latest valid code, and that one rule is applied in every step that uses subsectors.

How the build runs



Build steps and the files they pass to one another. An arrow means the later step reads a file the earlier step writes.


The build has 30 steps in five layers:

Geography (step 01). The county spine, CBSA crosswalk and annual population. Almost every later step reads it.
Nonprofit sources (02–09, 24).

BMF registrations (02, 02b, 08).
Financial returns: CORE (03), SOI (03b, 04), e-file (05).
Grants paid (09a, 09) and government grants (24).
Step 02 also writes the NTEE lookup that the later steps use.

Nonprofit panel (06). Filers, grassroots, registered stock and spending by county and year, plus market competition (23) and population-lag kernels (26).
Covariates (07, 11–22, 25, 27). Each reads only the geography, so their order does not matter.
Assembly (30). Merges everything into county_year and cbsa_year.

Order dependencies. Every file passed between steps is declared in pipeline.csv. The runner refuses to start if a step would read a file that a later step writes. Several dependencies used to be hidden and are now explicit:

step 02b reads the BMF cache that step 05 fills;
step 08 reads 02b’s ruling cohorts;
the NTEE lookup flows from 02 to 02b, 06, 08, 23 and 24.

Part 4 walks through running the build.


Known breaks in the series
Three breaks matter for analysis:

Source splices. CORE → SOI in 2011 and SOI → e-file in 2020 move spending SAMIs, but not counts. Filer counts for tax year 2020 are about 9% low.
Group exemptions. A few metros (Memphis, Mankato) are inflated by group-exemption subordinates registered at one address.
Interpolated covariates. Periodic sources are observed only in some years:

elections every 4 years;
the religion census every 10;
the social capital index 4 times;
the Census of Governments every 5.

Each comes in _obs, _lin and _locf versions (Part 3).

Use year fixed effects in every panel model, and check any change across 2011 or 2020 against counts before reading it as real (Part 7, Fact 7).

title: 0. Motivation
text:
The question communities ask
Local foundations, community foundations, United Ways and city and county governments spend heavily on their nonprofit sectors. They fund organizations directly, contract with them for services, and invest in capacity-building, leadership programs and shared infrastructure. Behind that spending sit three practical questions:

Is our nonprofit sector large or small for a place like ours?
Which local conditions go with a stronger sector, and which of them can we change?
How long should it take for an investment to show up in the sector’s size?

The research literature should help answer them, but in practice it gives a funder little to act on.


Why the evidence has not been usable
Nonprofit density has been studied for three decades. The theories are well developed: - Government failure: nonprofits supply public goods where preferences are diverse (Weisbrod, 1977). - Contract failure: nonprofits are trusted where quality is hard to judge (Hansmann, 1980). - Interdependence: government and nonprofits act as partners (Salamon, 1987).
The empirical tests disagree. Poverty, diversity, income and government spending have each been reported as positive in some studies and negative in others. In one panel of metro areas, the sign changed between pooled and fixed-effects models (Lecy & Van Slyke, 2013).
A funder reading this literature cannot tell whether the disagreements describe real differences between communities, or the many design choices each study made:

which organizations to count;
how to adjust for population;
whether to compare places or changes over time;
which unit and estimator to use.

Every one of those choices is defensible, and together they form a “garden of forking paths” (Gelman & Loken, 2014). A single study reports one path through it.
Two further problems make simple comparisons misleading:

Size. Bigger places have more of nearly everything. Counts of nonprofits grow in proportion to population, but spending does not (Bettencourt et al., 2007). Comparing per-capita spending across places of different size therefore ranks them by size.
History. A community’s nonprofit sector today largely reflects its past. Density is nearly frozen over decades. Without accounting for history, the effect of inherited size gets attributed to whatever current conditions correlate with it.



What this project does
The project addresses these problems in three steps:

A national database (Parts 2–4). It counts every 501(c)(3) public charity in every US county and metro area, 2000–2024, and joins them to about 300 covariates. Every input is frozen so that the database can be rebuilt exactly.
A fair benchmark (Parts 5 and 7). Each place is compared with its size-expected level, using scale-adjusted metropolitan indicators (Bettencourt et al., 2010). Seven stylized facts describe what any analysis of the data has to confront.
A multiverse (Parts 6, 8 and 9). Rather than choosing one design, the analysis fits every defensible combination of choices: about 432,000 specifications (Steegen et al., 2016; Young & Holsteen, 2017).

It reports which conclusions hold under all of them, and which decisions change the answer.
It then reads ten well-known studies through those results, to show why they disagree and where they agree.




What a community can take from it

A benchmark that compares like with like: density relative to places of the same size, not raw counts per resident.
A list of robust and fragile associations.

Robust, positive under nearly every design: education, civic participation and the sector’s history.
Fragile: the result depends on which organizations are counted and which question is asked, as with diversity and poverty.

Realistic expectations: density changes slowly, so sector-building goals and evaluations need long horizons.
A research agenda (Part 10): the data, methods and analyses needed to move from association to evidence about what local action can change.

title: 1. Literature review
text:
This project draws on three bodies of work. The first explains why some communities have more nonprofits than others. The second, urban scaling, sets the yardstick: how many nonprofits a place of a given size should be expected to have. The third, multiverse analysis, makes visible how much a conclusion depends on the analyst’s choices. Together they answer a practical question for local foundations and governments: compared with places like it, is our nonprofit sector large or small, and which of the levers we control are actually associated with a stronger sector?

Nonprofit density
Why nonprofits exist. Economic theories explain the nonprofit sector by the limits of markets and governments:

Government failure. Government supplies public goods at the level the median voter wants. Where preferences are diverse, nonprofits supply the unmet demand (Weisbrod, 1977).
Contract failure. Where donors or clients cannot judge quality, the nondistribution constraint makes nonprofits more trustworthy providers than firms (Hansmann, 1980).
Interdependence. Voluntary action has its own failures: it is insufficient, particularistic, paternalistic and amateur. Government and nonprofits therefore act as partners, with public money flowing through nonprofit providers (Salamon, 1987).

Each theory implies a different set of local conditions associated with a larger sector: demand heterogeneity, information problems, or government spending.
Empirical tests across places. A line of studies tests these theories by comparing nonprofit counts or spending across states, metros and counties:

the joint size of the for-profit, nonprofit and government sectors (Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen, 1992);
the growth of social-service nonprofits (Corbin, 1999);
metropolitan nonprofit sectors in NCCS data (Bielefeld, 2000);
community variations in the size and scope of the sector (Grønbjerg & Paarlberg, 2001);
a state panel test of government-failure theory (Matsunaga & Yamauchi, 2004);
social capital and sector growth (Saxton & Benson, 2005);
socioeconomic diversity and political engagement across counties (Kim, 2015);
government support and density in a metro panel (Lecy & Van Slyke, 2013).

Inconsistent results. The covariates in these studies are much the same: education, income, poverty, diversity, philanthropy, government, civic culture. Yet their signs often disagree from study to study. Poverty and income, for example, change sign between pooled and fixed-effects models of the same metros (Lecy & Van Slyke, 2013).
Studies also differ in many design choices:

whether they count organizations or dollars;
whether they scale by population, and how;
the unit of analysis;
the years covered;
the estimator.

The disagreements could therefore come from the communities or from those choices, and the literature has had no way to tell which. That gap motivates the rest of this project.


Urban scaling and SAMIs
Scaling laws. Many urban quantities grow as a power of population, \(Y = Y_0 N^{\beta}\) (Bettencourt et al., 2007; West, 2017):

Superlinear (\(\beta > 1\)): innovation, wages and GDP grow faster than population.
Sublinear (\(\beta < 1\)): infrastructure grows more slowly.
Linear (\(\beta \approx 1\)): individual needs, such as housing and jobs, grow in proportion to population.

The exponents are explained by the way social interactions grow with city size (Bettencourt, 2013) and are linked to a production-function view of cities (Lobo et al., 2013).
SAMIs. If density were judged by raw counts per capita, the result would depend on whether the outcome scales linearly. Scale-adjusted metropolitan indicators (SAMIs) solve this: each city’s deviation from the scaling line, the log of observed over size-expected (Bettencourt et al., 2010). - Independent of size. SAMIs remove size from the comparison by construction. - Persistent. A city’s SAMI changes slowly over decades. - Meaningful. They separate local performance from the effect of size.
Per-capita ratios have a known flaw. They are biased whenever the numerator does not scale one-for-one with the denominator, and they can induce spurious correlations between ratios that share it (Uslaner, 1976).
Cautions. - Estimated exponents are sensitive to the definition of the unit and the estimator, and apparent nonlinearity has to be tested, not assumed (Leitão et al., 2016). - Cross-sectional exponents need not describe how any one city changes over time (Bettencourt et al., 2020; Depersin & Barthelemy, 2018).
Both cautions recur in our design: the unit of analysis, the estimator, and cross-sectional versus within-city identification are decisions in the multiverse (Part 6, D2–D5).
What it means for nonprofit density. Counts of 501(c)(3) organizations scale almost exactly linearly with population at every unit of aggregation, but spending does not (Part 7, Fact 1). A metro’s filer SAMI is therefore a size-neutral measure: how many nonprofits it has relative to a typical place of its size. That gives local funders and governments a fair benchmark, comparing like with like rather than a small town with a large city.


Multiverse analysis
The problem. Every estimate depends on a chain of defensible choices. Leamer (1983) argued for reporting how estimates move across reasonable specifications. Later work showed how undisclosed flexibility produces false positives (Simmons et al., 2011), and that even analysts who never search for results walk a “garden of forking paths” (Gelman & Loken, 2014).
The method. - Multiverse analysis fits every combination of defensible choices and reports the whole set (Steegen et al., 2016). - Specification curve analysis adds inference across the set (Simonsohn et al., 2020). - Multimodel analysis attributes the spread of an estimate to the choices that produce it (Young & Holsteen, 2017). - Which choices to fork. Not every choice belongs in one distribution. Choices that change the question (non-equivalent) should be separated from arbitrary ones (Del Giudice & Gangestad, 2021).
Evidence that it matters. - When many teams analyse the same data to answer the same question, their estimates vary widely: in sign, size and significance (Silberzahn et al., 2018). - Much of that variation cannot be traced to any team’s identifiable choices (Breznau et al., 2022).
Density research fits this description. It has standard covariates, many defensible designs and conflicting published signs.
How this project uses it. - Design. The multiverse separates non-equivalent decisions (what question is asked: filers or spending, metros or counties, levels or changes) from arbitrary ones (how a construct is measured, which estimator, how gaps are filled). Each decision has a card with its options and a recommendation (Part 6). - Execution. It fits about 432,000 specifications on one common yardstick (Part 8). - Reporting. It reports which decisions move results and which covariates hold up under all of them.


What this means for local funders and governments
The three literatures together suggest how a community can assess its nonprofit sector:

Benchmark against size, not per capita. Compare a place with its size-expected level (its SAMI), not with raw counts per resident. Fact 1 shows counts scale linearly but spending does not, so per-capita spending comparisons mislead.
Expect slow change. Density is persistent over decades (Fact 2), and growth leaves a lag that closes slowly (Fact 3). A sector’s size today largely reflects its history. Goals and evaluation horizons should match.
Act only on robust associations. A factor that changes sign under reasonable alternative designs is not a reliable lever. The multiverse shows which local conditions are associated with a larger sector under every defensible design, and which are artefacts of a particular one.
Distinguish filers from grassroots. Most registered charities never file a full return (Fact 4). They respond to different conditions from established filers, so policies aimed at one group may not reach the other.

title: The Multiverse Approach
text:
Most disagreement in nonprofit density research comes from a few design decisions, not from the data. Studies that choose differently about the outcome, its functional form, the unit of analysis, the identification strategy and how covariates are measured can reach opposite conclusions from the same metros. A multiverse analysis makes those choices visible: it fits every defensible combination and asks which choices move the answer and by how much. This section explains how our multiverse is built (605,352 specifications over 387 metros, 2000–2024, run v10) and the three statistics used to read it.

Why a multiverse
Every empirical result rests on a chain of choices: which organizations to count, how to scale by population, which year, which estimator, which measure of each construct. Each choice is defensible on its own, and the chain branches at every step. Gelman and Loken (2014) call this the garden of forking paths. A single published estimate is one path through it, and readers cannot tell whether a neighboring path would have given the same answer.
Leamer (1983) proposed reporting how estimates move across reasonable specifications rather than choosing one. Multiverse analysis (Steegen et al., 2016) and specification curve analysis (Simonsohn et al., 2020) apply the idea systematically: define the set of defensible choices in advance, fit every combination, and report the whole distribution. Young and Holsteen (2017) add a decomposition that attributes the spread of an estimate to the choices that produce it.
Density research is a strong case for the approach. Its covariates are standard (education, poverty, diversity, philanthropy, government, civic culture), but published signs disagree. Racial diversity is positive in some studies and negative in others; poverty and income flip sign between pooled and fixed-effects models of the same metros (Lecy & Van Slyke, 2013). The paper asks whether those disagreements are about the world or about the paths taken.
The paper makes four contributions:

Seven empirical facts about density data that any design has to confront (01-stylized-facts.qmd).
A theory-based set of key variables, with a decision between single items and indexes for each construct (02-variables.qmd).
A decision card for each design choice: options, mechanism, evidence and recommendation (04-design-decisions.qmd).
A ranked summary of decisions by consequence, read on a common yardstick of benchmark covariates (05-findings.qmd).



Three kinds of decisions
Not every choice belongs in one distribution. Del Giudice and Gangestad (2021) distinguish choices that change what is being estimated from choices that are interchangeable ways of estimating the same thing. Pooling both into one specification curve produces a spread that has no interpretation. We tag every decision with one of three types, because the right response differs:



Table 1: Decision types.











Type
What it means
How it is handled
Examples




Estimand choice
The options answer different questions
Separate strata, never pooled; justified by theory
Outcome population, identification, unit of analysis


Analyst discretion
Defensible alternatives for the same question
Crossed as forks; report robustness across them
Estimator, year, winsorizing, measure of a construct


Avoidable error
One option is wrong for a known reason
Kept in the grid to show its cost, then excluded from recommendations
Per capita outcomes when the scaling exponent is far from 1; raw dollar predictors; OLS on outcomes with many zeros








The specification grid
A specification is one path through four layers of choices (Figure 1).






flowchart TB
  D["Data: 387 metros and 925 CBSAs, 2000–2024"]
  S["Strata (12, never pooled)<br/>construct (counts, spending) ×<br/>hospitals and universities (included, excluded) ×<br/>identification (cross-section, pooled, within)"]
  F["Forks, crossed within each stratum<br/>outcome measure · DV form (6) · predictor form (4) · log P on the right (2)<br/>unit (2) · estimator (4) · year (2, cross-section only) · winsorizing (2)"]
  C["Covariate sets (34)<br/>default model · drop one block (5) · swap one measure (15) · add one measure (13)"]
  X["Remove impossible pairs and algebraic duplicates"]
  R["605,352 specifications<br/>each gives a partial r for every covariate"]
  D --> S --> F --> C --> X --> R




Figure 1: One specification is one path through every layer of choices. Estimand choices split the universe into strata; analyst choices are crossed inside each one.





Strata. Choices that change the question split the universe into 12 strata that are never pooled: the construct (counts of organizations or spending), whether hospitals and universities are included, and the identification strategy (a single-year cross-section; a pooled panel, 2015–2022, with year fixed effects; or a within-metro panel, 2010–2022, with metro and year fixed effects).
Forks. Inside each stratum the defensible alternatives are crossed with each other:



Table 2: Forks crossed within each stratum.









Fork
Options




Outcome measure
Counts: filers, registrations (BMF). Spending: expenses or revenue, gross or net of grants to other organizations


DV form
Per capita; log per capita; log-log; SAMI; Poisson with a population offset; Poisson with log P free


Predictor form (size-scaled covariates)
Raw; per capita; logged; residualized on log P (SAMI form)


Log P on the right
No; yes


Unit
Metro; metro + micro


Estimator
OLS; state fixed effects; Census division fixed effects; state random effects


Year (cross-section only)
2022; 2019


Winsorizing
None; top and bottom 1%






Covariate sets. Covariates are organized in theory blocks with one default measure each. The covariate fork changes one thing at a time from the default model: drop one block (5 sets), swap one block’s measure for an alternative (15), or add one measure to the full default model (13: the pre-1970 endowment, two population-lag kernels, two civic measures, two religion measures, metro inequality, congregations, three indirect-government measures and direct government spending). With the default, that makes 34 sets. One-at-a-time changes keep the grid interpretable: each specification differs from a default twin in a single, named way.
Removing duplicates. Some combinations cannot apply (log-log needs log P on the right; Poisson models do not take state random effects; the within stratum uses only metro and year fixed effects; time-invariant covariates drop out under metro fixed effects). Others are algebraically identical: log(Y/P) with log P on the right equals log Y with log P on the right, and residualized predictors alongside log P equal logged predictors (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell). Duplicates are removed from the distribution and fitted only as a check. What remains is 605,352 specifications.
The grid grew in stages, and each addition was appended so earlier specification ids never changed: the 396,264 specifications of runs v5–v6, then 36,168 population-lag, 66,000 civic and religion, 34,584 inequality and congregation, and 72,336 government specifications (run v10).


One metric across all specifications
Coefficients cannot be compared across the grid: a per capita model, a log model and a Poisson model put the same covariate on different scales. Every specification therefore reports the partial correlation of each covariate,
r = \frac{t}{\sqrt{t^2 + df}}
with t from robust or clustered standard errors and degrees of freedom counted in metros. Partial r is scale-free across DV forms, identical across algebraically equivalent specifications, and a direct transformation of the t-statistic. As a rough guide, |r| ≈ .1 is small and ≈ .3 moderate.
What partial r measures. It is how closely a covariate tracks density once the other covariates are held fixed. % BA shows how different that is from the raw association (Figure 2).






Figure 2: What partial r measures. (A) Filer-count SAMI against % BA, bivariate: r = .59. (B) The same, net of the other covariates and log population, on the same scale: partial r = .26.




Bivariate (panel A). Across 387 metros in 2022, the filer-count SAMI rises 0.26 log points (about 30% more organizations than expected for size) per 10 points of % BA; r = .59.
Partial (panel B). Remove from both % BA and the SAMI what the other five covariates and log population predict, then plot the residuals around their means. The slope falls by more than half, to 0.11 per 10 points, exactly the % BA coefficient in the full model (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell). The correlation of the residuals, the partial r, is .26.
Semi-partial. Residualizing only % BA and correlating it with the raw SAMI gives .16. Its square (.025) is the share of total density variance that % BA explains on its own, a different question from the one the tables ask.
What control does to the data. More than half of the variance in % BA is shared with the other covariates: its SD falls from 8.8 to 5.6 points. Metros move along the x-axis: Eagle Pass, TX has a low raw % BA but a high value once its other traits are accounted for.

The tables compute partial r from robust or clustered t-statistics, so their values differ slightly from the residual correlation shown here (.24 vs. .26 for this model).


Reading one covariate across the grid
A single estimate tells readers little. Across the 55,912 specifications in one stratum (counts, cross-section), the partial r of % nonwhite runs from about −.5 to +.25 (Figure 3). The median is −.02, 61% of specifications share its sign, 31% are negative and significant, and 8% are positive and significant.






Figure 3: Specification curve for % nonwhite across the 55,912 specifications in the counts, cross-section stratum. The strips below show where each fork’s options fall along the curve.



The strips under the curve show where each option’s specifications fall. Dark means that option makes up most of the specifications in that part of the curve; read each row left to right, and the rows of one fork sum to 100% at every point.

Outcome (D1): filers sit at the negative end and registrations at the positive end.
Unit (D2): metro specifications fill the negative end; adding micro areas moves estimates toward zero and above.
Everything else has milder pulls: OLS leans negative and state random effects positive (D9), and models without log P on the right lean negative. DV form, predictor form, year, winsorizing and covariate set are spread evenly along the curve.

For every covariate the summary statistics are the median partial r, sign agreement (the share of specifications with the median’s sign), and the share significant at p < .05 under robust and under state-clustered standard errors.


Attributing the spread to decisions
The specification curve shows that a covariate moves; η² says which decision moves it. Each cell of the decision table answers one question: if you knew only which option of one decision a specification used, how much of the covariate’s spread could you predict?
\eta^2 = \frac{\sum_k n_k\,(\bar r_k - \bar r)^2}{\sum_i (r_i - \bar r)^2}
The numerator is the spread between option means; the denominator is the total spread across specifications. The example uses the 964 default-model specifications for filer counts in the cross-section (Figure 4).






Figure 4: η² for two decisions. Partial r of % nonwhite in 964 default-model specifications (filer counts, cross-section), grouped by estimator (η² = .15) and by winsorizing (η² = .01). Grey dots are specifications; the dashed line is the overall mean; orange dots are option means.




Grouped by estimator, the specifications separate partly. OLS averages −.15, division FE and state random effects −.08, and state FE −.06. Those four means account for 15% of the total variance: η² = .15.
Grouped by winsorizing, nothing separates. Both means sit on the overall mean: η² = .01.

The decision tables compute η² within each stratum and outcome, then average. Because some options only occur together, cells overlap and do not add up. η² is a marginal measure in the spirit of Young and Holsteen’s (2017) model influence: it says how much a decision matters for a covariate, not why.


The yardstick and the decision cards
Five benchmark covariates, fixed before any card was written, serve as the yardstick in every card: % BA, foundation assets, % nonwhite, turnout and poverty. Each stands for a theory the field tests and for a different way results go wrong (size scaling, measurement, estimator, collinearity); 02-variables.qmd defines them. Reading every decision on the same five covariates lets readers compare the cost of decisions directly.
Each design decision is written as a card with the same five parts, so the paper can be scanned as a reference:



Table 3: Parts of a decision card.

Each card reports, for each benchmark, the median partial r under each option, sign agreement, the share significant (robust and state-clustered), and the decision’s η². Results that matter but do not warrant a fork (the 2018 tax law, city-size heterogeneity, sample exclusions) are reported as sensitivity notes in 05-findings.qmd.

text:
Recommendation. A unified panel model of nonprofit density needs 13 covariates, one item per construct, with diversity and government split into the separate constructs they actually contain. Demand side: poverty, % 65+, the metro Gini, % nonwhite, religious fractionalization and age SD. Supply side: foundation assets, % BA and turnout. Market niche: a 10-year growth kernel, state and local government earnings (direct government), Medicaid receipts (indirect government) and the pre-1970 endowment. No VIF in this set exceeds 4.5. It explains 79% of filer SAMI variance in 2022 (62% grassroots, 45% spending). Composite indices beat the dominant item for no construct once interpretability and sign stability are counted. Collinearity is a problem only inside constructs: 12 pairs of candidate measures correlate above .7, and all are twins of one another.
The evidence below covers 387 metros, 2010–2022, with three outcomes: filer SAMI (n_filer_c3), grassroots SAMI (registered minus filers) and spending SAMI excluding hospitals and universities. Covariates are in model form: dollar totals and counts in SAMI form (log, residualized on log population by year, with the per-capita floor for zeros), rates as is, incomes logged. Log population stays on the right of every model. Partial r counts degrees of freedom in metros. The spending series was corrected on 2026-11-17 (e-file NTEE codes backfilled, so hospitals and universities are excluded in 2020–24); the tables below predate the fix, and refitting the lean model on the corrected series moves no spending partial r by more than .04.

Across 24 terms and six outcome-by-sample cells, 42 term-cells stay significant with the same sign, 44 are absorbed, 19 flip sign, 8 emerge and 31 are null in both (Figure 4).

Survive everywhere: % BA and the endowment. % BA falls from .44 to .30 for filers (2022) and stays significant in all six cells. The endowment falls from .51 to .32 and does the same. S&L earnings holds at .22–.25 for filers.
Absorbed: the Gini, congregations, turnout for filers. The Gini drops from .43 to .01 for filers; % BA is its main absorber (without % BA it is .20 pooled). Congregations drop from .31 to .02, absorbed by religious fractionalization. Turnout for filers drops from .17 to .04, again through % BA; for grassroots it holds (.34 → .27).
Flip: Medicaid, contributions, census response. Medicaid is negative alone (−.14 for filers) and positive combined (+.18; +.21 pooled). Alone it stands in for low education and fast growth (r −.37 with % BA, −.52 with the growth kernel). Contributions go from −.25 to +.05. Census response goes from .01 to −.17 once % nonwhite and turnout are in. Political division (+.09 to +.18 alone) and % foreign-born (+.12) go to zero or below.
