Where items are twins, the index equals the item. Growth, need and education/affluence have high α, and their indices give back the dominant item’s estimate. The item is simpler and keeps its unit.

What the lean model says.

Supply and history carry levels. % BA, the endowment, foundation assets and S&L earnings are positive for every outcome. Per SD, % BA moves filer density 17 log points and spending 31; the endowment moves them 10 and 13.
Indirect government matters for filers and spending, not grassroots. Medicaid is .25 and .16; for grassroots it is .01.
Heterogeneity splits by outcome. % nonwhite is negative for filers (−.20) and spending (−.09) but positive for grassroots (.12). Religious fractionalization drives grassroots (.52) and barely touches spending. Registered congregations sit inside the grassroots count, so part of that link is mechanical.
The endowment and growth history are one fact in levels. With the endowment in, the growth kernel is about −.05; without it, −.22. Within metros the kernel is −.20 either way. This qualifies D8’s advice to include growth history in every current-conditions model: in levels it is redundant with the endowment; within metros it is the main term.
Poverty depends on income. Adding per capita income moves poverty for filers from −.28 to −.12, the Gini from .13 to .05 and foundation assets from .22 to .16. Poverty also reverses with metro size: negative below about 250,000 residents, positive above (R/86, R/90). Report it as heterogeneity, not as a fork.

The historic size of the sector washes out under metro fixed effects. The endowment is fixed in 2000 and the BLS share moves 1.8% within metros over 2013–2022. With metro fixed effects both are absorbed, and the endowment’s SAMI form varies only with log population, which carries no information about history. So a within model cannot estimate history and cannot be confounded by it. It also cannot say why some places are dense. The cross-section and pooled panel can, but every resource coefficient there partly reflects history: without the endowment, foundation assets rise from .22 to .29 and S&L earnings from .23 to .29. Report both.

title: 8. Running the multiverse
text:
Note



Draft, 2026-11-18. Run times are still to be added from the build machine’s logs.


Part 5 explains why the analysis is a multiverse, and Part 6 sets out the decisions it crosses. This page shows how the multiverse is executed: the code that defines and runs the grid, the commands, the output files, and how the outputs become the findings. The approach follows multiverse and multimodel analysis (Simonsohn et al., 2020; Steegen et al., 2016; Young & Holsteen, 2017), and keeps choices that change the question apart from arbitrary ones (Del Giudice & Gangestad, 2021).

The run in one picture





flowchart LR
  P["cbsa_year.parquet<br/>(Part 2)"] --> G["40_multiverse.R<br/>grid + model engine"]
  G --> R["44_run_universe.R<br/>432,432 specifications<br/>in resumable batches"]
  R --> O["specs.parquet<br/>coefs.parquet"]
  O --> S["97_v11_decision_summary.R<br/>importance, stability"]
  O --> M["98_decision_matrix.R<br/>decision matrix figures"]
  S --> F["Findings<br/>(paper/05)"]
  M --> F








The engine: R/lib/40_multiverse.R
One file defines the whole universe. It has three parts:

The covariate catalog. Every covariate belongs to a block, a construct (need, heterogeneity, wealth, education, social capital, government, history, growth). Each covariate has a type:

Type A, intensive: rates and levels, such as the poverty rate. In the all-SAMI arm these are residualized on log population.
Type B, extensive: totals that grow with size, such as foundation assets. These enter raw, per capita, logged or as SAMIs.

Every block has a default measure plus alternatives. The current run uses the lean default model of 13 covariates (MV_MODEL=lean; Part 6, Variables).
The specification grid. The grid is built in three layers:

Strata: choices that change the question are never pooled. That means the construct (counts or spending), whether hospitals and universities are included, and identification (cross-section, pooled panel or within-metro).
Forks: inside each stratum, the arbitrary choices are crossed with each other: outcome measure, DV form, predictor form, log population on the right, unit, estimator, year and winsorizing.
Covariate sets: each fork combination is fitted with the default model, with one block dropped, with one measure swapped, or with one measure added.

Impossible combinations are removed, and so are specifications that are algebraic duplicates of another (for example, by the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem).
The model engine. One function fits a specification and returns one row per term: estimate, standard error, t, p, standardized β, n and R². Every covariate is compared on one yardstick, its partial correlation \(r = t / \sqrt{t^2 + df}\). Models are fitted with fixest (Bergé, 2026).



The scripts







Script
Role




R/lib/40_multiverse.R
catalog, grid and model engine (sourced by the others)


R/lib/41_composites.R
composite-index alternatives (unit-weighted z-score means)


R/multiverse/42_timing_test.R
sizes the grid and times 1,000 sampled specifications to estimate total run time


R/multiverse/43_verify_duplicates.R
checks that dropped algebraic duplicates give the same coefficients as their kept twin


R/multiverse/44_run_universe.R
runs a universe in resumable parallel batches


R/multiverse/45_summarize_run.R
first-pass summary: sign stability, share significant, variance decomposition


R/multiverse/46_compare_runs.R
compares two runs on their shared specifications


51, 53, 57
add an estimator (Census-division fixed effects), the composite indexes, or a longer within-metro window to a finished run


55, 82, 85, 92, 93
add-on covariate blocks: endowment, population-growth kernels, civic capacity and religion, inequality and congregations, government delivery mode


R/multiverse/97_v11_decision_summary.R
decision importance (η²), option medians, stability and drop-one-block shifts


R/multiverse/98_decision_matrix.R
the decision-matrix figures: one row per covariate, one column per decision



The add-on scripts append their specifications after the base grid, so the IDs of existing specifications never change, and a finished run can be extended without being re-run.


Running it
The multiverse is the multiverse stage of pipeline.csv, so it runs with the same runner as the database (Part 4):
Rscript run.R multiverse
That runs three steps, each with MV_MODEL=lean:








Step
Command it runs
Output




44v11
44_run_universe.R principled 2000 14 principled_v11
data/spec/run_principled_v11/: specifications in batches of 2,000, on 14 workers


97
97_v11_decision_summary.R
data/outline/v11/mv/: decision_importance.csv, option_medians.csv, stability.csv, drop_shift.csv


98
98_decision_matrix.R principled_v11
the decision-matrix figures



44_run_universe.R takes four arguments:
Rscript R/multiverse/44_run_universe.R <universe> <batch_size> <workers> <run_name>

universe: principled (the designed grid) or kitchen (every combination; built but not run).
batch_size and workers: how many specifications per batch, and how many run in parallel.
run_name: the output folder.

Each worker writes its batch to data/spec/run_<run_name>/batches/, and finished batches are skipped on a re-run, so an interrupted run resumes. At the end the batches are combined into:

specs.parquet: one row per specification, with its fork settings and status (432,432 rows in run v11);
coefs.parquet: one row per specification × term;
run_summary.csv.

Before a full run, 42_timing_test.R times a stratified sample of 1,000 specifications, serially and in parallel, and extrapolates the total run time.


From outputs to findings
Two summary scripts turn the coefficient table into the exhibits in the findings chapter:

Decision importance (97). For each covariate and decision, η² is the share of the spread in partial r across specifications that the decision explains, computed within strata. With 10⁴–10⁵ specifications every F test is significant, so η² ≥ .06 (a medium effect), not a p-value, marks a decision that matters.
Matched pairs (98). Pairs of specifications that differ in only one decision give two measures:

the mean absolute change in partial r;
the share of pairs whose verdict changes: significantly positive, not significant, or significantly negative.


What the run shows. Across the 13 covariates:

The question matters most. Choices that change the question change 20–42% of verdicts: which population is counted, how the model is identified, and the unit of analysis.
The usual robustness checks matter least. The choices papers usually report as robustness checks move the average covariate by .04 or less: the year, winsorizing, log population on the right, and the money measure.

The full tables, the decision matrix and the sensitivity analyses are in Findings.


Reproducing a run

Build the database (Part 4), or restore cbsa_year.parquet.
Rscript run.R multiverse. A full run is CPU-bound, and the number of workers is the third argument of step 44v11 in pipeline.csv.
Compare with the published run: specs.parquet and coefs.parquet should match specification by specification. Compare by specification ID, since parallel batches can finish in a different order.



References


Bergé, L. (2026). fixest: Fast fixed-effects estimations (Version 0.14.2) [Computer software]. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=fixest


Del Giudice, M., & Gangestad, S. W. (2021). A traveler’s guide to the multiverse: Promises, pitfalls, and a framework for the evaluation of analytic decisions. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 4(1).


Simonsohn, U., Simmons, J. P., & Nelson, L. D. (2020). Specification curve analysis. Nature Human Behaviour, 4(11), 1208–1214.


Steegen, S., Tuerlinckx, F., Gelman, A., & Vanpaemel, W. (2016). Increasing transparency through a multiverse analysis. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(5), 702–712.


Young, C., & Holsteen, K. (2017). Model uncertainty and robustness: A computational framework for multimodel analysis. Sociological Methods & Research, 46(1), 3–40.

title: 9. Reconciling the density literature
text:
Note



Draft, 2026-11-18. The details of each study come from the full text where it was available, and otherwise from the abstract and from how later papers describe it.

Read in full (7): Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen, Corbin, Bielefeld, Grønbjerg & Paarlberg, Matsunaga & Yamauchi, Saxton & Benson, Lecy & Van Slyke.
Abstract, plus later papers’ descriptions (3): Marquis et al., Kim, Bae & Sohn. Details marked unverified could not be confirmed and should be checked before the page is cited.
Interpretation: the mapping of each study onto the multiverse decisions is ours, and it is an argument, not a re-estimation of their models.

title: 9. Reconciling the density literature
section: Poverty: the sign depends on the question
text:
Poverty: the sign depends on the question

The studies:

Negative across places:

child poverty in Indiana counties (Grønbjerg & Paarlberg, 2001) and in Bae & Sohn (2018);
Lecy & Van Slyke’s pooled OLS;
Bielefeld (2000): across 9 metros, higher poverty goes with a smaller share of human-service providers (rank correlation −.38 for center-city poverty);
Corbin’s bivariate correlation, which he reports as significant and of the unexpected sign.

Positive:

Lecy & Van Slyke’s fixed-effects models (Lecy & Van Slyke, 2013);
unemployment, as a need proxy, within states in Matsunaga & Yamauchi (2004);
Corbin’s regression coefficient (Corbin, 1999), estimated on raw counts with no population term.


The multiverse:

Poverty is a robust negative covariate for filers across places: median partial r −.17, sign agreement 98%, significant in 86% of specifications.
It is weak for grassroots (−.07).
Within metros, it is near zero for filers (−.02) and turns positive for grassroots (+.08).
At the county level with metro fixed effects it turns positive, because organizations locate where need concentrates inside a market (D2).

Reconciliation: the negative and positive findings answer different questions.

Across places, poorer communities have fewer nonprofits for their size.
Within a market, or as poverty changes over time, organizations follow need.
Lecy & Van Slyke’s sign flip between OLS and fixed effects is this distinction inside a single paper. Matsunaga & Yamauchi’s positive unemployment effect is also a within-state estimate.
Corbin’s poverty sign also flips: negative alone, positive once size-correlated covariates enter a model of raw counts. That is consistent with size rather than need driving the regression coefficient.


Consensus: yes, once the question is stated. Across places the poverty sign is negative. The positive “need” effect is a location and timing effect, not a level effect.

title: 9. Reconciling the density literature
text:
Diversity: two populations, two signs

The studies:

Positive:

Corbin (1999): number of denominations, strongly positive; racial entropy, positive at p < .05 one-tailed. Both are on raw counts.
Bae & Sohn (2018): racial diversity (abstract only).
Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen, for education.
Bielefeld (2000): the most and least heterogeneous of 9 metros have the largest and smallest sectors. The metros in between show no pattern.

Negative:

Grønbjerg & Paarlberg (2001): number of denominations, for all, advocacy and mutual-benefit organizations.
Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen, for social services (Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen, 1992).

Null: Matsunaga & Yamauchi (2004) find racial heterogeneity not significant, with the unexpected sign, within states. Their positive heterogeneity result is for age heterogeneity.
Different construct: Kim reports a positive association for income inequality (Kim, 2015).

The multiverse:

% nonwhite has opposite signs for the two outcome populations: −.07 for filers and +.11 for grassroots. Each sign holds in 83–98% of specifications.
Religious fractionalization is a strong grassroots covariate (+.28, positive in 100%) but weak for filers (+.09).
Pooling the two populations puts % nonwhite near zero.
The measure also matters (D7): fractionalization behaves differently from counts of groups.

Reconciliation:

Population. Grønbjerg & Paarlberg count registered organizations, which are mostly grassroots. Studies of filers or employment (Lecy & Van Slyke; Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen; probably Bae & Sohn) measure the established sector. The two populations answer to diversity in opposite directions.
Measure and size. The number of denominations is a count that grows with population. See the callout above.

Against Corbin’s raw-count outcome it is positive by construction.
Against Grønbjerg & Paarlberg’s per-capita outcome it is negative, because smaller counties are denser per capita in their data.
Neither result isolates diversity (D4, D6). Fractionalization, which does not grow with size, is the measure the multiverse uses.

Identification. Matsunaga & Yamauchi’s null race result is a within-state estimate. Racial composition changes slowly, so state fixed effects absorb most of its variation. In the multiverse, % nonwhite also loses its cross-place sign within metros (−.10 for filers, −.08 for grassroots).
Subsector. Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen’s opposite signs for education and social services illustrate D11: heterogeneity findings are subsector-specific.


Consensus: emerging but conditional. Preference heterogeneity, measured as fractionalization, goes with more grassroots organizations. Its relationship with the established, filing sector is weak and can be negative. Diversity claims should name the population and the measure.

title: 9. Reconciling the density literature
text:
Income and education: resources matter

The studies:

Income positive across places:

Bielefeld (2000): rank correlation of wealth with filers per 10,000, .63;
Saxton & Benson (2005);
Lecy & Van Slyke (2013);
Corbin (1999): significant on raw counts, but in his words of “negligible” magnitude.

Income negative:

within states, in Matsunaga & Yamauchi (2004): a 1% rise in income per capita goes with about 0.7% fewer filers per capita;
Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen (1992), where the outcome is the nonprofit share of employment, not its size.

Education is positive in Grønbjerg & Paarlberg (2001) and in Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen outside health.

The multiverse:

% with a BA is the most robust covariate in the data. For filers it has a median r of .32, the same sign in 100% of specifications, and is significant in 100%. For spending it is .24, and for grassroots .15.
Foundation assets are positive for filers (.11, 86% agreement).

Reconciliation: the negative results answer different questions.

Share, not density. Richer places can have more nonprofits and a smaller nonprofit share of employment, if the for-profit sector grows faster.
Within, not across. Matsunaga & Yamauchi ask what happens as a state’s income rises, holding the state fixed. In the multiverse, % BA also shrinks within metros, from .32 to .08 for filers. Resource advantages show up across places, and they build slowly.


Consensus: yes. Education, and to a lesser degree wealth, go with denser nonprofit sectors under nearly every design. It is the most stable finding in both the literature and the multiverse.

title: 9. Reconciling the density literature
section: Government: complement, with a caveat on measurement
text:
Government: complement, with a caveat on measurement

The studies:

Complements: government grants in Lecy & Van Slyke (2013), federal spending in Saxton & Benson (2005), federal and local funding in Bae & Sohn (2018), and complementary financing in Matsunaga & Yamauchi (2004).
Null: federal funding in 1.
Negative: government wages in Lecy & Van Slyke.
Mostly no displacement: Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen (1992).

The multiverse:

Direct government (state and local government earnings) is modestly positive across places for filers: .09, 82% agreement.
Within metros it is near zero for filers (−.01) and negative for grassroots (−.13).
Indirect government (Medicaid, money paid through providers) is weak and fragile for filers: .03, 59% agreement. It is somewhat stronger for spending: .05 across metros and .08 within them.
Government grants received by nonprofits were left out of the panels, because they are mechanically tied to the outcome: more organizations receive more grants.

Reconciliation:

Measurement. The strongest “complement” findings measure grants received by the nonprofits being counted. That variable is partly an outcome, and on its own it cannot separate cause from accounting.
Identification. Lecy & Van Slyke’s government-wage term is negative. Whether that holds in their pooled models, their fixed-effects models or both is unverified. Our within-metro estimates for direct government are also zero or negative. Across places, larger government payrolls go with slightly more filers. As government grows within a place, there is no gain.
Delivery channel. Government support appears to work through money paid to providers, not through government size as such, but that channel is the measure most likely to be endogenous.


Consensus: partial. No study finds that government crowds nonprofits out. Whether government causes growth is unresolved, and it is the open question most relevant to public funders (Part 10).

title: 9. Reconciling the density literature
section: Religion, civic life and social capital
text:
Religion, civic life and social capital

The studies:

Church density or religious cohesion is positive in Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen (1992) and in Corbin (1999)’s regression. Corbin’s church density is negative in the bivariate correlation and positive only in the model of raw counts.
Political engagement is positive in Saxton & Benson (2005) and



Trust is negative in Saxton & Benson.
Associations or membership groups are null in Bae & Sohn (2018) and Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen.

The multiverse:

Turnout is a strong grassroots covariate (+.20, 100% agreement) and modest for filers (+.08).
It survives within metros (+.07 for filers, +.10 for grassroots).
Social-capital indexes that include association counts partly count the outcome.

Reconciliation:

Civic participation predicts the grassroots sector most clearly. Saxton & Benson study foundings, the flow most like grassroots, and find engagement positive.
Null association measures are expected when the index overlaps the outcome.


Consensus: yes for participation (turnout, engagement) and grassroots organizations. Generalized trust and association counts do not add.

title: 9. Reconciling the density literature
text:
Population and history

The studies:

Smaller counties are denser per capita in Grønbjerg & Paarlberg (2001).
Counts rise at a decreasing rate in Lecy & Van Slyke (2013), with population and its square as controls.
Existing density predicts foundings in Saxton & Benson (2005).

The multiverse:

Counts scale with population with an exponent of about 1.00 at the metro level (Fact 1), so per-capita counts are a fair metro yardstick. County-level per-capita densities are distorted by small denominators and group exemptions.
The pre-1970 endowment, the sector’s inherited size, is among the strongest covariates: .21 for filers and .19 for grassroots.
Density is nearly frozen over decades (Fact 2).

Reconciliation:

History. Saxton & Benson’s positive existing-density term is the same persistence the endowment captures. Models without history attribute part of the inherited level to whatever covariates correlate with it (D8). That includes region-linked ones such as diversity and income.
Size. The apparent density advantage of small counties is partly a feature of county units and per-capita measures (D2, D4).

title: 9. Reconciling the density literature
section: Government: funding complements, provision may substitute
text:
Government: funding complements, provision may substitute

The studies:

Money paid to nonprofits, positive:

government grants in Lecy & Van Slyke (2013);
federal spending in Saxton & Benson (2005);
federal and local funding in Bae & Sohn (2018);
“public subsidies” in Matsunaga & Yamauchi (2004). Their measure is total public support from the 990s, which, as they note, includes individual giving.
State welfare generosity (AFDC share) correlates .53 with sector size across 9 metros (Bielefeld, 2000).

Government’s own provision, negative (a substitute):

state and local direct spending, as a share of gross state product, within states in Matsunaga & Yamauchi: a 1% rise goes with about 0.22% fewer filers per capita;
government wages in Lecy & Van Slyke.

Null: federal funding in Grønbjerg & Paarlberg (2001). Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen find mostly no displacement (Ben-Ner & Van Hoomissen, 1992).

The multiverse:

Direct government (state and local government earnings) is modestly positive across places for filers: .09, 82% agreement.
Within metros it is near zero for filers (−.01) and negative for grassroots (−.13).
Indirect government (Medicaid, money paid through providers) is weak and fragile for filers: .03, 59% agreement. It is somewhat stronger for spending: .05 across metros and .08 within them.
Government grants received by nonprofits were left out of the panels, because they are mechanically tied to the outcome: more organizations receive more grants.

Reconciliation:

Measurement. The strongest “complement” findings measure grants received by the nonprofits being counted. That variable is partly an outcome, and on its own it cannot separate cause from accounting.
Identification. The substitution findings are within-place estimates:

Matsunaga & Yamauchi’s direct-spending result, from state fixed effects;
Lecy & Van Slyke’s government wages (whether pooled, fixed effects or both is unverified).

The multiverse shows the same pattern for direct government. Across metros, larger state and local payrolls go with slightly more filers (+.09). Within metros the association is zero for filers (−.01) and negative for grassroots (−.13). Places with big governments have big nonprofit sectors, but as a government grows, it does more itself.
Delivery channel. What complements the sector is money paid to providers, not government size as such. That is also the measure most likely to be partly an outcome.


Consensus: emerging, with a distinction. - Funding: government money that flows to nonprofits goes with larger sectors. - Provision: within places, government’s own provision tends to substitute for them.
Whether public funding causes sector growth is unresolved, and it is the open question most relevant to public funders (Part 10).
